# Initialization {#sec-init}

In this section we load packages. The hypergeometric function
$_{1}F_{1}$ is computed via the `gsl` package (GNU Scientific Library),
which provides a fast, vectorized `C` implementation.

```{r}
#| label: initialization
#| output: false

pacman::p_load(
tidyverse,  # Data processing and visualization
MASS,       # For mvrnorm() function
gsl,        # Fast C implementation of hypergeometric functions
gt          # Create tables
  )
```

# Background

Teunis [@teunis2022] has published new parameter estimates for a
*Salmonella* dose response model, based on an extensive data set
including experimental challenge studies of humans well as outbreaks.
The outbreak data were first published in a risk assessment by the
WHO/FAO Joint Expert Meeting on Microbial Risk Assessment
[@worldhealthorganization2002] and were modeled previously by the same
author [@teunis2010]. Individual challenge studies were modeled earlier
as well [@teunis1996]. The most recent analysis presents a joint
analysis of all data, using hierarchical Bayesian models as published
earlier for *Campylobacter jejuni* [@teunis2018] and also corrects a
data entry error in [@teunis2010]. Estimates are available for different
serovars of *Salmonella*. The model equations are:

*Infection*

$$p_{inf} = 1-_1F_1(\alpha,\alpha+\beta,-D)$$ {#eq-dr-inf}

where $p_{inf}$ is the probability of infection at an average dose $D$,
$_1F_1$ is the Kummer hypergeometric distribution of the first kind, and
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the shape parameters of the Beta-distributed
single hit probability.

*Illness conditional on infection*

$$p_{ill|inf} = 1-(1+D/\eta)^{-\rho}$$ {#eq-dr-ill-inf}

where $p_{ill|inf}$ is the probability of illness given infection at an
average dose $D$, and $\rho$ and $\eta$ are parameters describing the
Gamma distributed variability between hosts in clearing infection.

*Illness*

$$p_{ill} = p_{inf} \times p_{ill|inf}$$ {#eq-dr-ill}

where $p_{ill}$ is the unconditional probability of illness at an
average dose $D$.

The models were fitted using parameter transformations as follows:

*Infection*

$$u_1=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}; w_1=log(\frac{u_1}{1-u_1})$$ {#eq-inf-tr-w}

$$\nu_1=\alpha+\beta; z_1=log(\nu_1)$$ {#eq-inf-tr-z}

*Illness conditional on infection*

$$u_2=\frac{\rho}{\rho+\eta}; w_2=log(\frac{u_2}{1-u_2})$$ {#eq-ill-tr-w}

$$\nu_2=\rho+\eta; z_2=log(\nu_2)$$ {#eq-ill-tr-z}

Supplementary Table D.12 in @teunis2022 provide statistics on the joint
bivariate normal distribution of the dose-response parameters for these
models. This script provides code to reconstruct pairs of samples of the
dose-response parameters from these joint distributions for
implementation in risk assessment models. Outbreak data are preferred
over challenge experiments because they better reflect naturally
occurring exposures.

For implementation in R, the bivariate normal distribution is available
in the *MASS* package and the hypergeometric function in the *gls*
package. Equations for back transformation of the fitted parameters to
dose response parameters are:

$$\beta = \frac{e^{z_1}} {1+e^{w_1}}; \alpha =\frac{e^{z_1}}{1/e^{w_1}+1}$$ {#eq-btr1}

$$\eta = \frac{e^{z_2}} {1+e^{w_2}}; \rho =\frac{e^{z_2}}{1/e^{w_2}+1}$$ {#eq-btr2}

See XXX for derivation of these equations.

# Functions

::: callout-note
The optimization of the implementation of the hypergeometric dose-response model to prevent numerical underflow was generated by Posit Assistant (Claude Sonnet 4.6), and checked by the
author.
:::

$P(\text{inf} \mid d)$ is computed using the confluent hypergeometric
function $_{1}F_{1}$, implemented in the `gsl` package via the GNU
Scientific Library. The `gsl`
implementation accepts vectorized inputs and runs at C speed, producing
identical results to double-precision accuracy to an alternative high precision implementation in the Python `mpmath` library.

At very high doses and for posterior samples with large parameter values
($a \sim 100$, $b \sim 10{,}000$), `hyperg_1F1` can underflow to `NaN`
rather than 0. Because $P(\text{inf} \mid d) \to 1$ in this regime,
these values are replaced with 0 before subtracting from 1.

```{r}

# Hypergeometric infection dose-response model
p.inf.hyp1f1 <- function(a, b, D) {
  val <- hyperg_1F1(a, a + b, -D)
  # At very high doses, hyperg_1F1 can underflow to NaN rather than 0;
  # the true value is 0 (p_inf = 1) at these extreme doses.
  val[is.nan(val)] <- 0
  1 - val
}

# Hazard-based illness-infection model
p.ill.inf <- function(n, r, D) {
  1-(1 + D / n)^(-r)
}

# Parameter back transformations
par1.btr <- function(w, z) {
  exp(z) / (1 + 1 / exp(w))
}

par2.btr <- function(w, z) {
  exp(z) / (exp(w) + 1)
}
```

# *Salmonella* Typhimurium (outbreak data)

# Infection model

```{r}
set.seed(2730)
n_samp <- 10000 # sample size
mu <- c(-2.83, 3.83) # means for S. Typhimurium Table D.12
covar <- matrix(c(3.89, -3.40, -3.40, 4.36), ncol = 2) 
# covariance matrix (var(w), covar(w, z), covar(w, z), var(z)) Table D.12
# sd <- apply(abs(covar), c(1,2), sqrt) * sign(covar)
samp_inf_tm <- mvrnorm(n = n_samp, mu = mu, Sigma = covar) # calculate samples
samp_inf_tm <- as.data.frame(samp_inf_tm) %>%
  mutate(a = par1.btr(V1, V2), b = par2.btr(V1, V2))
```

## Illness \| infection model

```{r}
mu <- c(-5.13, 3.77) # means Table D.12
sigma <- matrix(c(2.94, -2.84, -2.84, 3.93), ncol = 2) # covariance matrix Table D.12
samp_ill_tm <- mvrnorm(n = n_samp, mu = mu, Sigma = sigma) # calculate samples
samp_ill_tm <- as.data.frame(samp_ill_tm) %>%
  mutate(r = par1.btr(V1, V2), n = par2.btr(V1, V2)) # back transformation
```

## Comparison of summary statistics of reconstructed samples and published model

Comparison of means, 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles from reconstructed samples
with summary statistics in Table D1 of [@teunis2022] is provided for the
dose-response parameters(alpha, beta, eta, rho).

```{r}
# Infection
comp_inf_tm <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("mean_sample", "mean_fit",
                "P2.5_sample", "P2.5_fit",
                "P97.5_sample", "P97.5_fit"),
  alpha = c(mean(samp_inf_tm$a), 4.5,
        quantile(samp_inf_tm$a, 0.025), 0.151,
        quantile(samp_inf_tm$a, 0.975), 23.1),
  beta = c(mean(samp_inf_tm$b), 225,
        quantile(samp_inf_tm$b, 0.025), 0.134,
        quantile(samp_inf_tm$b, 0.975), 1280)
  )

# Illness | infection
comp_ill_tm <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("mean_sample", "mean_fit",
                "P2.5_sample", "P2.5_fit",
                "P97.5_sample", "P97.5_fit"),
  rho = c(mean(samp_ill_tm$r), 0.718,
        quantile(samp_ill_tm$r, 0.025), 0.033,
        quantile(samp_ill_tm$r, 0.975), 4.11),
  eta = c(mean(samp_ill_tm$n), 144,
        quantile(samp_ill_tm$n, 0.025), 0.272,
        quantile(samp_ill_tm$n, 0.975), 794)
  )

# Merge and print results
comp_tm <- left_join(comp_inf_tm, comp_ill_tm)
comp_tm |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(md("Comparison of mean values of reconstructed samples and fitted values from published paper, *S*. Typhimurium")) |> 
  tab_options(
    heading.title.font.size = px(16))|>
  fmt_number(
    columns = -statistic,
    n_sigfig = 3,
  )
```

## Save data

```{r}
samp_tm <- cbind(samp_inf_tm[, 3:4], samp_ill_tm[, 3:4])
write.csv(samp_tm, "samp_tm.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Plot models

```{r}
#| warning: false

colors <- c("Infection" = "blue", "Illness | Infection" = "orange", "Illness" = "red")

dr_mod_tm <- samp_tm %>%
  mutate( id = 1:n() ) %>%
  expand_grid( tibble( dose = 10^seq(-2, 8, 0.1))) %>%
  mutate(p_inf_tm = p.inf.hyp1f1(a, b, dose),
         p_ill_inf_tm = p.ill.inf(n, r, dose),
         p_ill_tm = p_inf_tm * p_ill_inf_tm) %>%
  pivot_longer( c(p_inf_tm, p_ill_inf_tm, p_ill_tm), names_to="type", values_to="prob") %>%
  group_by(dose, type ) %>%
  summarize( best =median(prob),
             low = quantile( prob, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
             high = quantile( prob, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE ) ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c(low,best,high), names_to="quantile", values_to = "prob")

ggplot(dr_mod_tm) +
    geom_line( aes( x=dose, y=prob, color=type, linetype=quantile ) ) +
    scale_x_log10() +
ggtitle("Salmonella Typhimurium") +
labs(x = "Dose") +
ylab("Probability")
```

# *Salmonella* Enteritidis (outbreak data)

## Infection model

```{r}
set.seed(2730)
n_samp <- 10000 # sample size
mu <- c(0.0721, 0.00668) # means for S. Enteritidis Table D.12
covar <- matrix(c(2.26, -1.36, -1.36, 01.66), ncol = 2) 
# covariance matrix (var(w), covar(w, z), covar(w, z), var(z)) Table D.12
# sd <- apply(abs(covar), c(1,2), sqrt) * sign(covar)
samp_inf_ent <- mvrnorm(n = n_samp, mu = mu, Sigma = covar) # calculate samples
samp_inf_ent <- as.data.frame(samp_inf_ent) %>%
  mutate(a = par1.btr(V1, V2), b = par2.btr(V1, V2))
```

## Illness \| infection model

```{r}
mu <- c(-2.20, -0.0571) # means Table D.12
sigma <- matrix(c(0.7, -0.28, -0.28, 0.609), ncol = 2) # covariance matrix Table D.12
samp_ill_ent <- mvrnorm(n = n_samp, mu = mu, Sigma = sigma) # calculate samples
samp_ill_ent <- as.data.frame(samp_ill_ent) %>%
  mutate(r = par1.btr(V1, V2), n = par2.btr(V1, V2)) # back transformation
```

## Comparison of summary statistics of reconstructed samples and published model

Comparison of means, 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles from reconstructed samples
with summary statistics in Tables A.7,A.10 and A.12 of [@teunis2022] is
provided for the dose-response parameters(alpha, beta, eta, rho), the
slope of the dose response curves at low doses (\<\< 1 cfu, low_dose_inf
and low_dose_ill_inf), and the single hit probability (P_1) for
infection.

```{r}
# Infection
comp_inf_ent <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("mean_sample", "mean_fit",
                "P2.5_sample", "P2.5_fit",
                "P97.5_sample", "P97.5_fit"),
  alpha = c(mean(samp_inf_ent$a), 0.688,
        quantile(samp_inf_ent$a, 0.025), 0.0404,
        quantile(samp_inf_ent$a, 0.975), 2.73),
  beta = c(mean(samp_inf_ent$b), 1.34,
        quantile(samp_inf_ent$b, 0.025), 0.00218,
        quantile(samp_inf_ent$b, 0.975), 6.7)
  )

# Illness | infection
comp_ill_ent <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("mean_sample", "mean_fit",
                "P2.5_sample", "P2.5_fit",
                "P97.5_sample", "P97.5_fit"),
  rho = c(mean(samp_ill_ent$r), 0.146,
        quantile(samp_ill_ent$r, 0.025), 0.01223,
        quantile(samp_ill_ent$r, 0.975), 0.0666),
  eta = c(mean(samp_ill_ent$n), 1.16,
        quantile(samp_ill_ent$n, 0.025), 0.156,
        quantile(samp_ill_ent$n, 0.975), 3.63)
  )

# Merge and print results
comp_ent <- left_join(comp_inf_ent, comp_ill_ent)
comp_ent |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_caption(md("Comparison of mean values of reconstructed samples and fitted values from published paper, *S*. Enteritidis")) |> 
  opt_table_font(size = 14)|>
  fmt_number(
    columns = -statistic,
    n_sigfig = 3,
  )
```

## Save data

```{r}
samp_ent <- cbind(samp_inf_ent[, 3:4], samp_ill_ent[, 3:4])
write.csv(samp_ent, "samp_ent.csv", , row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}

ggplot(dr_mod_ent) +
```

# Appendix: derivation of backtransformation equations {.appendix}

$$ \frac{u_1}{1-u_1}=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}/(1-\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}) =\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}/\frac{\alpha+\beta-\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$$ {#eq-u1}

$$w_1=log(\frac{\alpha}{\beta});
\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=e^{w_1};
\alpha=\beta e^{w_1}$$ {#eq-w1}

$$log(\alpha+\beta)=z_1;\alpha+\beta=e^{z_1}$$ {#eq-z1}

$$\beta e^{w_1}+\beta=\beta(1+e^{w_1})=e^{z_1};\beta=\frac{e^{z_1}}{1+e^{w_1}}$$ {#eq-beta-btr}

$$\alpha=\frac{e^{z_1}}{1+e^{w_1}}e^{w_1}=\frac{e^{z_1}}{1/e^{w_1}+1}$$ {#eq-alpha-btr}
